candidates.title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
candidates.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents accomplish complex tasks through multi-turn interactions with external tools. However, malicious content embedded in user queries, tool descriptions, or environment observations can manipulate their decisions and induce unsafe actions. Adversarial co-evolution has emerged as an effective approach to strengthening LLM safety, but existing work primarily focuses on language-level safety or indirect prompt injection in web tasks. candidates.title: Constraining Tool Authority in AI Agents: A Risk-Tiered Framework for Mitigating Indirect Prompt Injection
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents read untrusted content, such as emails, web pages, and documents, and act through tools. Instructions hidden in that content can steer the agent, and the agent's permissions can turn that influence into unauthorized actions. This paper proposes a risk-based authorization architecture that reduces the consequences of indirect prompt injection without assuming the model resists it. candidates.title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
candidates.summary: LLM-based agents increasingly execute long-horizon, end-to-end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. candidates.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents interact with external resources to complete complex user tasks, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where malicious instructions redirect agents toward attacker-intended tasks. candidates.summary: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, where adversarial instructions embedded in external data sources manipulate agent behavior without direct user input. These external data can originate from user documents, web retrieval results, or API outputs, leading to unauthorized compliance, sensitive information disclosure, identity spoofing, and cross-agent propagation of unsafe practices. candidates.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. candidates.title: TRACER: Trace-Regularized Training Against Indirect Prompt Injection
candidates.summary: Indirect prompt injection uses untrusted retrieved content, tool outputs, or agent messages to override an LLM's intended behavior. We show that defense robustness is channel-conditioned: the same attack succeeds 18% of the time as a follow-up message but 53% when placed in retrieved context. We propose TRACER (Trace-Regularized Adversarial Channel Exposure with Reward-shaping), a channel-aware adversarial training method that samples presentation wrappers and combines an answer-anchored, evidence-gated reward with ATRC, which aligns attacked reasoning with clean evidence when an injection is invalid. candidates.title: Prompt-Injection Probes Learn the Conversation, Not Just the Injection
candidates.summary: Linear probes on a model's hidden states are used as cheap monitors for indirect prompt injection: they screen the tool outputs an agent reads and send suspicious ones to a slower second check, so every false alarm has a cost. candidates.venue: World Journal of Advanced Engineering Technology and Sciences
candidates.summary: Enterprise AI agents now read tickets, documents, and web pages and then act on what they find through tool protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP). candidates.title: Empirically Analyzing Web Privacy Defenses
candidates.summary: Privacy threats are abundant when a user browses the Web. For example, online tracking code collects information about people for targeted (and potentially discriminatory) advertisements. Governments have surveilled foreign and domestic network traffic. Attackers also forge criminal legal process documents (e.g., search warrants) to steal user data from tech companies. In response to these threats, privacy defenders have created tools that are sometimes widely adopted, but the threats still remain. candidates.title: Agents Break Together on Misuse, Apart on Injection
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.summary: Do safety breaches of computer-use agents co-occur across model families the way correctness errors do? Five agents from four vendors on 150 OS-Harm tasks, pre-registered, zero cost. On deliberate misuse the agents comply together (tetrachoric ρ 0.67, 1.4 effective votes of 5); on prompt injection which agent obeys is close to idiosyncratic (ρ 0.28, no task breaks all five); on the same tasks safety breaches are more shared than task failures (ρ 0.27–0.51).

candidates.summary: [EN] Agents based on large language models (LLMs) with access to external tools have become the standard architecture for production artificial intelligence systems.
